overview.title: Chorale no. 40
overview.summary: Chorale no. 40 belongs to the Baroque era — music by Johann Sebastian Bach.
overview.history: Chorale no. 40 is ready to explore on Lune. It is associated with Johann Sebastian Bach. Stylistically it sits in the Baroque world. Start by listening, then ask about the bars that surprise your hands. Place every phrase in the Baroque sound-world: how would someone from that time shape it?
highlights: Place every phrase in the Baroque sound-world: how would someone from that time shape it?

eraInfo.label: Baroque
eraInfo.story: Ornament, drive, and clear bass lines. Think dance rhythms, terraced dynamics (sudden soft/loud), and melodies that keep spinning forward.

composerInfo.name: Johann Sebastian Bach
composerInfo.hook: Bach builds beauty from clear lines that weave together.
composerInfo.bio: Listen for independent voices, steady pulse, and ornaments that sparkle without rushing. In preludes, let patterns bloom; in chorales, hear every voice.
composerInfo.full: Johann Sebastian Bach (1685–1750) shaped Baroque counterpoint into music that still trains every serious pianist. Listen for independent voices, steady pulse, and ornaments that sparkle without rushing. In preludes, let patterns bloom; in chorales, hear every voice.
highlights: Bach is closely tied to the piano — tone and touch are part of the story.

Dotted rhythm on G4 — subdivide and count the small beats aloud (“1-and-a, 2-and-a”) so the short note arrives exactly late, never lazy.
Both hands are active (4 right-hand and 3 left-hand attacks) — practise hands separately until each is easy, then join at half speed before returning to tempo.

rh: Line: D5 → G4 → C4 → B3 → F4 → C5 → E4 → G3
Right hand: wide stretch — keep the wrist soft and shift the arm, don’t poke.
Right hand: prepare leaps by looking at the landing note before you leave.
Right hand: dense bar — practise in groups of 3–4 notes, then glue the joins.
lh: Left hand: wide stretch — keep the wrist soft and shift the arm, don’t poke.
Left hand: prepare leaps by looking at the landing note before you leave.
together: Hands together only after each hand’s line is clean alone.
Listen for which hand carries the tune — that hand leads, the other supports.
Slow metronome: one hand alone → both hands at half speed → nudge the tempo up.

practiceNotes: Slow practice: one chunk clean, then add the next. Never rush the join.
Say the finger numbers out loud while you play each chunk.
For jumps: freeze on the landing note, then go back and add the leap.
Use a dotted rhythm on the run (long–short, then short–long) to lock the fingers in.
